PURPOSE: literature track I — explainability of machine-learned risk models, not just rule scorecards.
Cerneviciene & Kabasinskas: a systematic review of XAI in finance — SHAP and LIME dominate but are usually bolted on after training.
Nallakaruppan et al.: gradient-boosted models plus explainability layers keep their accuracy. Zhu et al.: ensemble accuracy and explainability tooling can coexist.
Lin & Wang: a caution — SHAP explanations can drift between retraining runs, so attribution stability must be monitored.
Takeaway: a calibrated model with SHAP is a realistic Phase 2 companion to our scorecards, provided we watch stability.

PURPOSE: literature track II — agentic / LLM document pipelines, and privacy-preserving learning.
Agentic side: Ali shows agentic AI (LLM + RAG + RPA) speeds up underwriting but leaves explainability and compliance open. Privacy side: the multi-bank federated study reaches near-centralized accuracy while keeping data local; Farooq et al. extend the same federated pattern to fraud detection.

PURPOSE: literature track III — fairness and governance, a dimension Phase 1 ignored entirely.
Bahlool, Hewahi & Elmedany review 43 studies: performance, fairness and explainability are usually optimized separately; fairness constraints are tunable and moderate ones cost little accuracy. Lesson: test fairness BEFORE adding a supervised model, not after.
Garcia-Llorente & Olmeda compare AI oversight across nine jurisdictions and give a three-level governance structure — individual rights, institutional accountability, systemic safeguards — aligned with the EU AI Act treating credit scoring as high-risk.
Mention that, with the agentic and LLM papers added, the survey now totals 27 references.

text:
PURPOSE: synthesise where LoanLens still differs from the literature — four points.
One: most explainability is post-hoc; few pair it with bounded rule scorecards like we do, so Phase 2 compares the two directly.
Two: agentic and LLM systems trade privacy and auditability for fluency; we keep inference local and borrow only their auditability ideas.
Three: federated learning solves a data-sharing problem we do not yet have, but its privacy techniques are reusable later.
Four: fraud research favours black-box ensembles that are hard to justify to an officer; Phase 2 tests whether a calibrated model plus SHAP can match a scorecard's transparency.
Bottom line: keep the local, explainable core and layer research-backed upgrades on top.

1) Build a governed, de-identified, labelled dataset with train/validation/test splits — everything else depends on this. 2) Train and calibrate supervised models and compare them against the scorecards on the same data. 3) Add SHAP-style attributions once the model choice is validated.
4) Activate the fraud model by connecting or replacing the offline Isolation Forest. 5) Harden security — JWT/SSO, RBAC, encryption, audit logging. 6) Add oversight — model monitoring, drift checks, and adverse-action reason codes.

text:
PURPOSE: the NEW Track 4 — the optional agentic-AI enhancement the guide asked for.
Be explicit that this is OPTIONAL and ADVISORY, scoped in Phase 2 and prototyped only if time allows — it is not a rewrite of the system.
What the agent would do (left): classify and read each document and extract fields; flag missing or inconsistent paperwork; retrieve the relevant policy text using agentic RAG; and draft a plain-language summary of the evidence.
Guardrails that keep it safe (right): it is barred from the Approve/Review/Reject decision; every tool call is written to the processing log; a human officer reviews and can override it; and active scoring stays local.
Close on the box: this design is grounded in the agentic-AI papers added to the survey — Okpala et al. [21], Singh et al. [22], Ferrag et al. [23] — so we gain the speed of agentic document handling while containing its auditability cost. The decision always stays with the scorecards and the officer.

PURPOSE: Track 2 — security and production readiness.
Replace demo credentials with real authentication (JWT/SSO) and role-based access control. Encrypt data at rest and in transit and put raw-payload storage behind access controls.
Add structured audit logging, secrets management, and retention/deletion policies. Move large batches and OCR to background workers so the system scales. Add adverse-action reason codes and policy checks aligned to lending regulation. Add model-drift monitoring with a lightweight model registry.
Note these map directly onto the three-level governance structure from the literature survey.
